issues.explanation: Carrying a weapon is hard to reconcile with the rest of this profile and trauma type. For a 61-year-old married male paramedic whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, the other selected items center on sensory triggers, intrusive recall, and emotion-focused coping. Weapon carrying implies a persistent interpersonal/assault threat context that is not represented in the triggers, memory, or formulation, making this item clinically incoherent here.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Intense shame on recall is weakly supported by the rest of the selected profile. The formulation shows Threat and Negative Appraisals as inactive, yet shame is a strong self-appraisal-based memory response. With no negative appraisal items and no threat-linked content, this item does not fit the otherwise trigger-memory-avoidance pattern as well as the other memory items.

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: For a toxic chemical exposure trauma, helicopter/aircraft sounds are hard to reconcile unless the exposure clearly occurred in an air-evacuation or aircraft-related context; nothing else in the profile supports that context, so this trigger appears trauma-incongruent.

Dark spaces are not impossible, but with toxic chemical exposure they are weakly supported here because no memory, threat, or appraisal content links the trauma to darkness or confined/obscured environments. In this profile the trigger set starts to imply a different trauma context than the rest of the items.

vignette:
Rajan is a 61-year-old South Asian man who has worked as a paramedic for over three decades, a career he once described as his calling. He is married and, by most outward measures, presents as composed and professionally seasoned. He was referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating distress that his wife had noticed over the preceding eight months, and which Rajan himself had struggled to name until recently.

The incident that precipitated his current difficulties occurred during a routine emergency call to an industrial facility. Rajan and his partner arrived to find a worker collapsed in a poorly ventilated storage area where a chemical coolant had been leaking for hours. The smell was sharp and medicinal - something between antiseptic and industrial solvent - and the space was dim, lit only by a single emergency strip light that cast long shadows across the floor. Rajan entered without full respiratory protection, a decision made in seconds under pressure, and within minutes he felt his eyes burning, his chest tightening, and a wave of disorientation that he initially mistook for exertion. It was only when he stumbled and his partner dragged him out that he understood something was wrong. He spent two days in hospital under observation. The medical team reassured him that there had been no lasting physiological damage, but Rajan left with something they could not measure on a chart.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not settle. It remained close to the surface, and certain things could bring it back without any warning at all - not gradually, but instantaneously and in full. The smell of rubbing alcohol on a colleague's hands, the particular quality of darkness in an unlit stairwell, the ambient sounds and smells of the ambulance bay itself: any of these could collapse the distance between then and now, returning him not to a recollection but to the experience itself, complete with the same terror he had felt on the floor of that storage room. When the memory returned this way, the emotional force of it was so overwhelming that he would have to stop whatever he was doing - mid-sentence, mid-task - unable to continue until the wave passed. Because the memory could be triggered without warning, Rajan began to experience his own workplace as a source of constant latent threat, and the ambulance, the bay, the equipment - things he had once handled with ease - became charged with the possibility of re-exposure.

It was the triggers themselves that began to organise his behaviour. To manage the risk of being ambushed by the memory at work, he started avoiding anything that might concentrate the exposure: he declined calls that involved hospitals when he could, found reasons to step back from physical examinations, and felt a creeping dread whenever a shift began. At the same time, the memory's capacity to overwhelm him when it surfaced led him to a strategy that felt, at first, like simple practicality: he made sure he was never alone. He filled every available space in his day with conversation, company, noise - surrounding himself with people so that the silence in which the memory tended to find him could not take hold. His wife noticed that he no longer sat quietly in the evenings, that he sought her company with an urgency that was different from affection. But the constant socialising, while it suppressed the memory's immediate return, also prevented him from processing what had happened, and so the memory remained unintegrated - ready to be triggered again by the next encounter with darkness, or the sharp chemical note of alcohol, or the interior of the vehicle he drove to work each day. The avoidance of medical settings, similarly, foreclosed any opportunity to build a different relationship with the context of the event, keeping the workplace and its associated cues perpetually threatening. Over months, the loop tightened: the triggers fed the memory, the memory sharpened his vigilance toward triggers, and the strategies that were meant to contain both instead preserved them.

He also found himself returning, in quiet moments that broke through despite his efforts, to the question of what he should have done differently - rehearsing the decision not to wait for full equipment, turning it over without resolution. This rumination, though not the centre of his distress, sat beneath everything else.

What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a near-miss at work: he froze at the entrance to a darkened corridor during a call, and his partner had to take over. He is most afraid, he says, that he has become unreliable - that the person he has been for thirty years is no longer there. What he hopes for, more quietly, is to be able to walk into a dark room without bracing for the floor to disappear beneath him.
